name: Rhyme-as-reason effect
statement: A saying that rhymes is rated as a more accurate description of human behaviour than the same saying reworded so that it does not rhyme.
meaning: The claim is about a rating, not about conduct. A participant reads a saying and marks on a scale how accurately it describes people. Replace one rhyming word with a synonym, so the line no longer rhymes, and the mark falls, although the two versions assert the same thing. The account offered for this is misattribution. Rhyme makes a sentence quicker and smoother to take in, and that ease gets read as a signal that the content is sound. None of the sayings used is checkable against anything, so what the scale records is how true a line feels.

origin.who: Matthew S. McGlone and Jessica Tofighbakhsh
origin.note: Their paper is "The Keats heuristic: Rhyme as reason in aphorism interpretation", and it carries the whole original experiment. The better-known publication is their 2000 paper in Psychological Science, "Birds of a feather flock conjointly (?): Rhyme as reason in aphorisms", which most secondary accounts cite as the source of the effect. Both authors were at Lafayette College, and the work was first presented at an American Psychological Society convention in May 1998.

evidence: The 1999 experiment took 50 rhyming aphorisms from two printed dictionaries and cut them to 30 after 20 students confirmed they were unfamiliar and that the rewrites did not change the meaning. Each aphorism had two non-rhyming versions, made by swapping either the first or the second rhyming word for a synonym, so "Woes unite foes" became "Misfortunes unite foes" and "Woes unite enemies". Sixty further undergraduates were given one of three lists, each holding 10 aphorisms in rhyming form and 20 in modified form, and rated all 30 on two 9-point scales. Mean accuracy was 6.38 for the rhyming forms against 5.15 and 5.33 for the two modified forms, Fp(2,118) = 9.15, p < .01, Fi(2,58) = 4.77, p < .02. The planned comparison of rhyming against modified gave Fp(1,118) = 7.54, p < .01 and Fi(1,58) = 3.91, p < .05, so the test treating aphorisms as the random factor is the weaker of the two. Comprehensibility was 7.06, 6.83 and 7.11, with no reliable difference, so the rhyming versions were not rated truer because they were easier to follow. Asked at the end whether rhyming aphorisms describe behaviour more accurately, all 60 said no. The 2000 Psychological Science paper was not obtained and only its abstract was read. That abstract reports the same accuracy advantage and adds that it was attenuated when participants were cautioned to separate a saying's poetic qualities from its semantic content, a caution the 1999 experiment does not contain. No sample size, mean or test statistic from the 2000 paper is quoted here.

examples.tag: The proverb on the kitchen wall
examples.text: 'Haste makes waste' is taken as a sound description of how people behave. 'Hurrying causes waste' asserts the same thing and is marked down. Nothing about the claim changed except how easily the line goes in.

A public health line that rhymes is treated as better founded than a plainer sentence carrying the same instruction. The rhyme makes the line quick to take in, and that ease is read as a sign the content has been checked.

examples.tag: The saying passed round a family
examples.text: A rule about weather or health circulates for years because it sits well in the mouth. Its standing comes from its form, and none of the people repeating it could say what it rests on.

replication.headline: No independent repeat of the aphorism experiment was found. The finding rests on 60 undergraduates at one American college rating 30 antique English proverbs.
replication.detail: The 2000 Psychological Science paper is McGlone and Tofighbakhsh reporting further work of their own, and its abstract describes a caution manipulation the 1999 experiment does not contain. It is a second run by the original authors rather than an independent test. The two studies usually offered as support are extensions rather than repeats. Filkuková and Klempe wrote new advertising slogans in 2013 and found, in their first experiment, that rhymes were rated more likeable, more original, easier to remember, more suitable for campaigns, more persuasive and more trustworthy. Their second experiment found social advertising rated favourably in both forms. Only in a third, within-subjects experiment, where the two forms sat on one scale, were rhymes clearly preferred on both form and content. Kara-Yakoubian and colleagues tested a different device in 2022, the A-B-B-A pattern of antimetabole, and found an accuracy advantage in three of four experiments with 797 people. Neither reuses the original materials or the original design, and neither is a test of rhyme in aphorisms.

limits: The search behind the none-located verdict covered Crossref and Europe PMC by title and DOI, a Europe PMC full-text search pairing the effect's two names with replication and preregistration terms, the citing lists of both original papers through Semantic Scholar, which on 21 September 2026 returned 294 works citing the 2000 paper and 33 citing the 1999 one, OSF projects and registrations, the Collaborative Replications and Education Project, and web searches for preregistered, student and classroom replications under both the 'rhyme as reason' and 'Keats heuristic' names. Nothing repeating the original design came back. Three documents could not be read on 21 September 2026, and in each case what turned the request away was a bot challenge rather than a paywall page. Sage answers requests for the 2000 paper with a Cloudflare bot challenge, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record that paper as closed with no repository copy. Wiley lists Filkuková and Klempe's article as open at the publisher and serves the same Cloudflare challenge, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and OpenAIRE record no repository copy. Elsevier lists Menninghaus and colleagues' article as open under a Creative Commons licence and answers with a captcha, and the Max Planck repository holds only a submitted version behind a bot check of its own. All three are used here through their abstracts alone, and the next reader may not meet these blocks. The tested materials were antique English proverbs unfamiliar to American undergraduates, and the rhyme turned on a single substituted word. Menninghaus and colleagues, working with proverbs that combine rhyme, metre and artful shortness, found those features made semantic comprehension harder while raising beauty and succinctness ratings, which is a more tangled picture than a single fluency dial.
misreadings: Johnnie Cochran is an illustration, not a result. He appears in the closing paragraph of the 1999 discussion, in the form "If the gloves don't fit, you must acquit", which is not the wording usually quoted, and no juror was measured in either paper. The outcome is a rated accuracy score, and persuasion, memory and behaviour are separate things. Filkuková and Klempe rated slogans for persuasiveness and trustworthiness rather than truth, and the older claim that rhyme aids recall is a different literature again. The name Eaton-Rosen phenomenon has no traceable origin. It entered the Wikipedia article on 11 July 2013 in an edit from an anonymous address, summarised as 'alternative nomenclature' and carrying no citation. Searches of Crossref and Europe PMC for the term returned no work on rhyme, and the Eaton-Rosen those indexes do return works on infant brain imaging. Every source found using the term postdates that edit.

sources.text: McGlone, M. S., & Tofighbakhsh, J. (1999). The Keats heuristic: Rhyme as reason in aphorism interpretation. Poetics, 26(4), 235-244. Full text read for this entry, including the appendix listing all 30 aphorism sets. Elsevier serves only the abstract; the copy read was the scanned journal offprint mirrored at gwern.net, which carries both authors' names, the Lafayette College address and the Poetics pagination.

McGlone, M. S., & Tofighbakhsh, J. (2000). Birds of a feather flock conjointly (?): Rhyme as reason in aphorisms. Psychological Science, 11(5), 424-428. Not obtained on 21 September 2026. Sage returns a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall page, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar record the article as closed with no repository copy. The abstract was read at PubMed, PMID 11228916. No sample size, mean or test statistic from this paper is quoted here.

Filkuková, P., & Klempe, S. H. (2013). Rhyme as reason in commercial and social advertising. Scandinavian Journal of Psychology, 54(5), 423-431. Unpaywall and OpenAlex list the publisher PDF as open, and Wiley answered every request for it on 21 September 2026 with a Cloudflare bot challenge, not a paywall. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and OpenAIRE record no repository copy. The abstract was read at PubMed, PMID 23841497, and no statistics from the article are quoted.

Kara-Yakoubian, M., Walker, A. C., Sharpinskyi, K., Assadourian, G., Fugelsang, J. A., & Harris, R. A. (2022). Beauty and truth, truth and beauty: Chiastic structure increases the subjective accuracy of statements. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology, 76(2), 144-155. The published abstract was read at PubMed, PMID 35266782, and is the source for the figures quoted here; a PsyArXiv preprint exists and was not used.

Reber, R., & Schwarz, N. (1999). Effects of perceptual fluency on judgments of truth. Consciousness and Cognition, 8(3), 338-342. Abstract read in full at PubMed, PMID 10487787; statements shown in high-contrast colours were judged true above chance, those in moderately visible colours at chance. That abstract gives no sample size, and the article is closed at its publisher.

Menninghaus, W., Bohrn, I. C., Knoop, C. A., Kotz, S. A., Schlotz, W., & Jacobs, A. M. (2015). Rhetorical features facilitate prosodic processing while handicapping ease of semantic comprehension. Cognition, 143, 48-60. Unpaywall and OpenAlex list the publisher PDF as open under a Creative Commons licence, and ScienceDirect answered every request for it on 21 September 2026 with a captcha, not a paywall. The Max Planck repository copy is a submitted version and sits behind a bot check. The abstract was read at PubMed, PMID 26113449, and no statistics from the article are quoted.

The diff against the previous revision shows the phrase 'or Eaton-Rosen phenomenon' being added to the opening sentence with no citation. Read as the artefact itself, not as an encyclopedia entry.
